name: Jade Petrov

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for talking with me, Jade Petrov. I am a researcher with the Work Futures Panel, independent of employers, unions, AI firms and parties. What you say is confidential. What is an ordinary shift like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I run the tile kiln at Vale Ceramics and check which trays are cooling too fast before we wrap a pallet. I've been the lead on that line for years, and the two-year technical diploma helps me understand the temperature trace, though I still lift tiles into the light. Tariq, my partner, repairs bicycles three days a week, our daughter is grown, and we have four months of bills saved while we pay a roof loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AI Plateau. "Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kiln crew to keep checking the edges by hand. A tidy AI log won't show a hairline split until someone lifts the tile into the light.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Four months of bills are set aside, and my kiln shift is regular, so this picture leaves me reasonably settled. Tariq's bicycle repairs are patchy in winter, which keeps me from calling the household rich.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep running the tile kiln and signing the cooling checks myself. From each full pay packet I'd add a little to the reserve before we spend on the roof loan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly steady, with the usual nag about winter repairs. I wouldn't lose sleep over a tool that only tidies paperwork.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which kiln check would you keep even if the AI log looked clean?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The back corner of a tile can cool faster and leave a tiny crack. I lift samples from both edges before I release a pallet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the roof loan cost you each month?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It takes a manageable slice of my pay, but I notice it when Tariq has a quiet week. Our grown daughter pays her own rent, so I don't count on her money.

say: I would keep **hand-checking tiles** because a clean log cannot show every hairline crack.
I would tell the crew that **ordinary work** continues while AI only tidies paperwork.
think: My **regular kiln wage** and four-month reserve make this mild picture manageable.
Tariq’s **winter repair income** varies, and the roof loan still needs paying.
do: **Keep** running the tile kiln and checking samples before releasing pallets.
**Add** new money from full pay packets to our reserve before spending on the roof.
feel: I feel **steady**, with ordinary worry about winter repairs.
S0.quote: A tidy AI log won't show a hairline split until someone lifts the tile into the light.
fieldNote: Jade trusts her **eyes and hands** because she names a particular crack the log might miss.
Her four-month reserve offers room, yet **winter bicycle repairs** and a roof loan make her careful.
She plans to save from **new wages**, not merely count the money already held.

steps.text: Keep running kiln and checking cooled tile samples before pallet release
Add new money from full pay packets to roof-loan reserve

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called Steady Disruption. "Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the team that planning software may cut office jobs before anyone touches the kiln. If the new camera is meant to reduce our inspection rota, the manager should put the hours in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A two-line roster could take away one of my paid checks each week, and Tariq's winter trade cannot cover the roof loan on its own. My diploma helps me read a temperature trace, but it does not make me qualified to isolate a robot arm.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask for the proposed rota and compare its paid hours with three recent slips. If the plant offers a funded course on paid time with guarded practice and a fitter beside me, I'd take the camera-control training; otherwise I'd keep my kiln role and watch the posted vacancies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious if that roster trimmed a shift. Four months saved is breathing room, not a replacement wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would count as a safe lesson on the new camera?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I need the machine stopped, guarded, and a fitter who can show me the isolation switch. A slide presentation in the canteen would leave me guessing at the live line.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask your daughter to cover the roof payment?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, she has her own bills and I am still earning. Tariq and I would first change our own spending if a shift really went.

say: I would ask for **written hours** before a camera changes the kiln inspection rota.
I would tell the crew that **planning software** reaches office tasks before the hot kiln.
think: A smaller **paid rota** could cut my wage while the roof loan continues.
My diploma does not prove **robot isolation** competence without guarded practice.
do: **Compare** the proposed paid rota against three recent wage slips.
**Take** funded camera-control training only with paid time and guarded fitter-led practice.
feel: I feel **anxious** about losing regular paid checks.
S1.quote: A slide presentation in the canteen would leave me guessing at the live line.
fieldNote: She separates a useful **temperature trace** from safe authority to isolate a robot arm.
Written paid hours matter because the **roof loan** cannot be met by irregular bicycle repairs alone.
Jade would accept the course only with an **offered funded place**, paid time and guarded practice.

steps.text: Compare proposed paid rota with three recent wage slips
Take offered funded paid camera course only with guarded fitter-led practice

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2028. "Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kiln crew that office orders could be automated by 2028, while physical tile handling faces the robots around 2031. We need notice and a paid route into safe maintenance, not a promise that everyone becomes a technician.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 63 when capable robots reach the kiln. If they take most inspection shifts, the four-month reserve and Tariq's repair takings won't bridge four years to my hoped-for stop at 67.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the employer for a real funded, paid maintenance place with supervised lockout practice and a recognised test. If accepted, I'd attend; after qualifying I'd apply only to posted local maintenance work with hours and net pay that cover the roof loan. If no place opens, I'd search for a posted tile-inspection shift at workable pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That one would keep me awake. I know four months in the account cannot turn a lost senior wage into a retirement income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before leaving this kiln for maintenance work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would need a posted job, a written wage after travel costs, and a safe isolation qualification. A new title with no paid shift behind it would do nothing for the roof payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you simply stop working at 63?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not checked what our income after work would really be. I would only stop if written figures for both of us covered housing, food and repairs.

say: I would press for **notice and paid training** before robot tile handling cuts the kiln crew.
I would explain that **thinking AI arrives first**, with hands-on robots roughly three years later.
think: At 63, lost kiln shifts could outrun our **four-month reserve** before a hoped-for stop at 67.
A **maintenance title** cannot pay the roof loan without a real local wage.
do: **Request** an offered funded, paid, recognised maintenance place with supervised lockout.
**Apply** after qualification only for posted local maintenance work at roof-covering net pay.
**Search** posted tile-inspection shifts if no course opens and pay remains workable.
feel: I feel **alarmed** and expect lost senior shifts to disturb my sleep.
S2.quote: A new title with no paid shift behind it would do nothing for the roof payment.
fieldNote: She expects a **major income loss** by the 2031 robot stage and explicitly says it would keep her awake.
Her planned retirement at 67 is a **hope**, conditional on written household income and costs.
Maintenance is conditional on a **real offered place**, paid practice, a safe credential and a posted adequate job.

steps.text: Take offered funded paid maintenance place only with supervised lockout and recognised test
Apply after qualification to posted local maintenance if net pay covers roof loan
Search posted tile-inspection shifts if no course opens and pay works

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2031. "Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the kiln crew the extra years are worth using, but no one should be taken off the roster for unpaid classes. A proper apprenticeship has to include stopped-machine practice, not a booklet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 66 in 2034 I might still need another year of kiln wages before retirement works. The longer notice gives me time to learn, but a certificate won't create a maintenance vacancy in one of our nearby plants.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd get written retirement income and roof-loan figures this year. If the plant offers a funded recognised maintenance apprenticeship on paid shifts with guarded lockout and a fitter supervising, I'd enrol; after passing, I'd apply to posted nearby work only if the net wage covers our costs. Without that place, I'd keep the kiln role while its paid shifts last and check posted inspection jobs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be anxious rather than sleepless, because there is time to check the sums. The part I can't settle today is whether a paid place and a job will exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the retirement figures say you can stop at 66?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I would compare the written income with housing, food and roof repairs before handing in notice. I won't name an exit date from a rough estimate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the apprenticeship unusable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Unpaid days or an unguarded robot would rule it out. Tariq's variable winter repairs cannot replace my wage while I sit in class.

say: I would insist on **paid guarded practice** before trusting a robot maintenance apprenticeship.
I would tell the crew that extra time helps only while **paid shifts** continue.
think: At 66, retirement still needs **written income** that covers our household costs.
A maintenance certificate needs a **posted viable vacancy** after training.
do: **Request** written post-work income and roof-loan figures this year.
**Enrol** only in offered funded paid apprenticeship with guarded supervised lockout.
**Apply** after passing for posted nearby maintenance at cost-covering net pay.
feel: I feel **anxious**, with time to plan but no guaranteed course or paid job.
S3.quote: A proper apprenticeship has to include stopped-machine practice, not a booklet.
fieldNote: Her outlook favours **proved apprenticeships**, but she rejects an unpaid or unsafe place.
An age-66 exit is not assumed; she asks for **written income and costs** before leaving paid work.
Jade separates an accepted course from a **posted maintenance wage** and a separate inspection fallback.

steps.text: Request written retirement income and roof-loan figures this year
Enrol only in offered funded paid apprenticeship with guarded supervised lockout
Apply after passing for posted nearby maintenance if net pay covers costs
Check posted inspection shifts if no course opens and pay covers costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The next picture is called AGI by 2036. "Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans." If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a decade can carry a good apprentice from novice to lead before robots handle the kiln. I would still ask the manager to show the pay and training places on paper.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 68 when thinking AI arrives and 71 when hands-on robots reach the kiln. I hope to stop full shifts at 67. Four months saved is not a pension, and my partner's winter repair income varies.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my present kiln post and ask for a full written retirement calculation with Tariq's reliable income and the roof loan included. If the figures cover living costs, I'd stop at 67 before the robots; if not, I'd seek a posted local inspection role only if I can still do it safely and its net wage covers the bills.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be uneasy, mainly about what the figures will say. There is time to find out, and I am not expecting this year's kiln pay to disappear.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you train for robots at 68 if you had already retired?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, if I had actually left full shifts and the income covered bills, there would be no need. If I were still employed, I would only take a funded paid guarded course that came with a real safe role.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell a younger operator on your shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell her to learn the temperature trace and the tile itself, then get a recognised qualification while the company will pay. The kiln still needs judgement today, even if its future is different.

say: I would ask for **written pay** and **training places** while the kiln still provides regular work.
I would tell apprentices that a decade can build **real kiln skill** before hands-on robots.
think: At 71, I may have retired only if **documented household income** covers our costs.
Four months saved and variable repairs do not become **permanent retirement income**.
do: **Keep** running the kiln while current paid shifts remain available.
**Request** written retirement figures and **stop at 67** only if household income covers costs.
**Search** posted local inspection work if retirement fails and safe net pay covers bills.
feel: I feel **uneasy** about retirement sums, with current work still secure.
S4.quote: Four months saved is not a pension, and my partner's winter repair income varies.
fieldNote: The long runway brings retirement within reach, but **actual written figures** decide whether Jade stops at 67.
She distinguishes current employment from a **conditional post-2036 job search** if retirement proves unaffordable.
She would not retrain after retirement; any late course would need a **funded paid guarded place** and a safe role.

steps.text: Keep running kiln while current paid shifts remain available
Request written retirement income and roof-loan costs before choosing exit
Stop full shifts at 67 only if documented household income covers costs
Search posted safe local inspection if retirement fails and net pay covers bills

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because robots reach tile handling around 2031, when I would be 63 and still need a wage. A funded paid place with supervised lockout, then a real posted job at workable pay, would give me a route.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: I would like you to ask who pays workers while they learn to make a robot safe. A technical diploma is useful, but the kiln arm does not care about a certificate unless I can isolate it properly.

headlineQuote: A technical diploma is useful, but the kiln arm does not care about a certificate unless I can isolate it properly.
portrait: Jade is a **58-year-old kiln lead** at Vale Ceramics with a two-year technical diploma and strong judgement about tile cooling.
Her household has **four months saved**, a roof loan, grown daughter and variable income from her partner Tariq’s bicycle repairs.
She is **steady with new tools**: she wants written hours, guarded practice and a fitter before trusting a camera or robot arm.
She hopes to stop at **67** only if verified income covers costs; earlier robots threaten needed kiln wages.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries me most because capable robots could remove my kiln shifts by 2031.
whatWouldHelp: An **offered funded paid course**, supervised lockout and posted work at a cost-covering wage would help.
